justification: Committed to B. The passage puts the lifting force in the shallow mats: “In the few centimetres directly beneath the stones – where the slab cools after sunset and moisture condenses on its underside … her team found dense mats of fine root, thickening year on year”, and Askerholt says “Most of the force, we think, is generated within a hand’s width of the stone.” A fails because she does settle the question rather than failing to; C overstates “there was almost nothing alive” into “entirely without roots”; D’s cut anchoring roots are never mentioned anywhere in the text.

Committed to D. The five are explicitly characterised: “They had been bedded to an older specification, on coarse sand laid nearly twice as deep as the current rule allows, and the roots had evidently found it worth living in.” A is contradicted twice – “The crates, not the soil, carry the weight of the traffic above” and root mats “riding clear over the crates beneath” (crates intact). B describes the separate single street where “a water main was renewed halfway along it”, which “failed and taught nobody anything”. C is directly contradicted by “The five had one thing in common.”

Committed to A. The closing paragraph is explicit that the good streets are only inferred from the surface: “The surveys measure the stones, and only the stones”, and Askerholt adds “We are reading the flags, not the roots … For all we know, the bedding on the good streets is filling with root that has not yet found its strength.” B is contradicted by “stayed within tolerance” plus the recorded “four millimetres” (movement exists, it is merely tolerable); C is an absolute the passage pointedly refuses; D is not addressed.

Committed to B. Fearnbeck predicted “The roots will cross the crates and settle in the bedding”, and on five streets the survey “found exactly what Fearnbeck had said it would find”, but on twenty-five it did not. The writer then judges in her own voice: “Askerholt’s group had thought his worry overdone. On the five streets the case is fairly won; on the twenty-five it is not” – vindicated on one point, unvindicated in general. A and C each take only one half of that sentence; D fails because “the case is fairly won … on the twenty-five it is not” is the writer adjudicating, not abstaining.

Committed to C. The text does two things and only two: it explains the mechanism – “The slab shades the ground, waters it every clear night and lets it breathe. It builds the very thing that lifts it” – and then reports how the root-cell remedy fared across “Thirty-one streets … rebuilt on cells” over seven years. A takes only the framing (“compensation for trips over lifted paving costs more each year”); B’s “finally beat” is contradicted by “The stones are behaving; that is all I will sign my name to”; D is not addressed at all.

Committed to C. The frame is “it quietly takes its ___(1)___ on the general mood”, and only “toll” completes the fixed collocation take its toll on, which also carries the required sense of slow cumulative damage matching “quietly”. “price” and “cost” are exacted or paid, not “taken … on” something; “charge” takes no such pattern at all.

Committed to D. The contrastive “but” and the target sentence set the surface against the intent: “The tone is light, but nobody misreads it; beneath the sponge the message is ___(2)___, and it is aimed at certain chairs.” Only “pointed” supplies the required sharpness-with-a-target that “aimed at certain chairs” demands. “relaxed” and “amused” restate the light tone and so destroy the contrast; “spirited” means lively, which is neither the contrast nor a property a written notice’s hidden meaning can have here.

Committed to A. “you cannot hold the moral high ___(3)___ and a dripping brush at the same time” is the fixed idiom the moral high ground, and the joke depends on the reader recognising it verbatim. “horse” belongs to a different idiom (get on one’s high horse) and cannot be held; “field” and “floor” produce no English phrase in this frame.

Committed to B. The two sentences are a wait and its resolution: “So the kitchen waits. ___(4)___, somebody cracks – nearly always the same somebody”, which requires the temporal “Eventually”. “Similarly” asserts a parallel that the preceding sentence does not offer; “Presumably” hedges a claim the writer immediately details as known fact; “Ironically” would need a reversal, and someone cracking after a wait is the expected outcome, not a reversal.

Committed to C. “most kitchens ___(5)___ an uneasy balance between confrontation and squalor” takes strike, the standard verb of strike a balance, and “uneasy balance” is its most common modifier. “cast”, “deal” and “land” each collocate with other objects (a vote, a blow, a deal, a punch) but none governs “a balance” in English.

Committed to A. Slaking is described directly: “Möter den brända stenen sedan vatten börjar den sjuda, spricker och faller sönder till ett fint vitt mjöl” – seething, cracking and crumbling to a fine white powder, which A paraphrases exactly. C reverses the chemistry: it is heat, not water, that expels the carbon dioxide (“När kalksten hettas upp till omkring tusen grader driver värmen ut koldioxiden ur stenen”). B’s moulds appear nowhere; D is contradicted because the stone disintegrates and still needs sand (“som blandad med sand ger murbruk”).

Committed to D. The organisation paragraph is unambiguous: “En ugn var för stor för ett enskilt hushåll. Den restes och brändes av ett ugnslag – en handfull grannar som sköt till var sin andel ved, turades om vid elden och delade den färdiga kalken efter insats.” A is contradicted by that same first sentence; B’s visiting professional burners are never mentioned – burning was “böndernas sak”; C is contradicted by “Det mesta av kalken gick till avsalu.”

Committed to B. Both halves of B are stated: the trade was a significant side income – “för många hushåll var ugnen den binäring som över huvud taget gav kontanter” – and its traces survive – “ett sjuttiotal ugnsrester bara i Klyvinge med grannsocknar: låga, övervuxna rösen av rödbränd sten”. A inverts the priority (“Fram för allt var det dit kalken gick: till murningen”, with only “något” reaching the fields); C overstates “för många hushåll” into a collapse of the whole rural cash economy; D is contradicted by “Berget var däremot sällan något bekymmer”.

Committed to C. The remains are described as successive rather than simultaneous: “inte sällan flera i rad utmed samma sluttning, äldre ugnar som övergivits när skogen omkring dem huggits ut och ersatts av en yngre ugn längre bort” – so a count of surviving remains overstates how many were in operation at any one time. D is directly contradicted by “Hur gamla de äldsta lämningarna är går inte att avgöra utan utgrävning”; A makes a national comparison the text never offers; B compares Klyvinge with its neighbouring parishes, which the text also never does.
